newsitem.title: CHINA: China boom prompts WFP shift in aid focus.
newsitem.headline: China boom prompts WFP shift in aid focus.

text.p: China's economic boom and years of bumper harvests are prompting the World Food Programme to shift its aid focus towards skills and training and away from direct food donations, a WFP official said on Wednesday.

The WFP last year shipped about 110,000 tonnes of grain to China, making Beijing the second largest recipient of the U.N. agency's direct assistance after Bangladesh, said WFP China country director Else Larsen.
"China is of course one of the countries where one has to begin to consider whether assistance is needed at the same level," Larsen said in an interview.

"If WFP can bring in skills and techniques, that could probably over the next years be more our role," she said. "We would like to try to work with the government to set a clear framework for gradually scaling down our direct assistance."

China's powerful development performance, with economic growth rates averaging over 10 percent over the last decade, has prompted calls from some Western donor nations for international aid to be funnelled elsewhere.

China counters such calls by arguing that tens of millions of farmers remain mired in grinding poverty despite the new prosperity of their urban compatriots, and Beijing has reacted sharply to any suggestion it is no longer eligible for aid.
The WFP did not plan to pull out of China, but ever-growing pressure on its scarce resources meant the focus of its assistance should change, Larsen said.

About one million Chinese are currently actively involved in WFP "food-for-work" programmes, under which they received around 3.25 kg (7.16 lb) of grain a day to labour on projects such as building terraced fields or improving irrigation systems.

The WFP had developed considerable expertise in targeting the most vulnerable communities and in focusing on women's development, and the agency hoped to continue to pass such skills to local Chinese authorities, Larsen said.

Smaller projects such as a new initiative in central Anhui province that had a relatively low price tag of $3.0 million and in which WFP took a smaller role could have a catalyst effect on Chinese development efforts, she said.
Other food-for-work programmes were already tied to agricultural credit schemes that could help to ensure beneficiaries did not slip back into poverty, she said.

Aid officials say China remains strongly opposed to any reduction of grain shipments from abroad, despite its economic boom and two years of bumper harvests that have left granaries bulging at the seams.

While Beijing is committed to grain self-sufficiency, donations from such nations as Canada, Australia, Germany, Japan and Norway are seen as helping a high-profile campaign to eliminate absolute poverty by 2000, the officials say.
China could consider using more of its stored grain to expand food-for-work style development programmes that targeted its poorest people, Larsen said.
Any scaling back of foreign food donations would be unlikely to have any great impact on China's overall grain trade, which has soared as demand for meat and processed food grows.
Even in relatively good harvest years, China needed to import from nine million to 30 million tonnes of grain -- an amount that dwarfed donations, Larsen said.
"One hundred thousand tonnes is a drop in the ocean," she said.
